title: Tower Tiles
statement: A clock tower's facade is a strip two tiles tall and length tiles wide. It is covered with identical 1 × 2 tiles, each placed either upright (covering a column) or flat (covering two side-by-side cells in one row), with no gaps or overlaps. Return the number of different tilings modulo 1000000007.

examples.explanation: Three upright tiles, or one upright tile plus a stacked pair of flat tiles on either side: 3 tilings.

hints.content: Look at the leftmost column of a tiling.
Either one upright tile covers it, or two flat tiles stacked on top of each other cover the first two columns.
So the tilings of length n split into those of length n - 1 and those of length n - 2.
ways(n) = ways(n - 1) + ways(n - 2), with ways(0) = ways(1) = 1.
Compute it bottom-up with two variables and apply the modulo after each addition; plain recursion repeats work exponentially.

testCases.explanation: Three upright tiles, or one upright tile plus a stacked pair of flat tiles on either side: 3 tilings.
Two upright tiles, or two flat tiles stacked.
The true count (1836311903) exceeds the modulus, so the answer is reduced modulo 1000000007.
A long strip that requires an iterative solution and the modulus.

solutions.title: Plain recursion
solutions.intuition: The first column is covered either by one upright tile or by a stacked pair of flat tiles.
solutions.approach: ways(n) returns 1 for n <= 1, otherwise ways(n - 1) + ways(n - 2) modulo 1000000007.
solutions.pseudocode: ways(n): if n <= 1: return 1; return (ways(n-1) + ways(n-2)) mod M
commonMistakes: Using ways(0) = 0, which makes every count wrong.
Expecting this to finish for large lengths; it recomputes the same subproblems repeatedly.
solutions.interviewExplanation: The recurrence is right, but without memoization the call tree grows like the Fibonacci numbers themselves.

solutions.title: Iterative two-variable recurrence
solutions.intuition: Each answer depends only on the previous two.
solutions.approach: Start a = ways(0) = 1 and b = ways(1) = 1, then roll forward length - 1 times with (a, b) = (b, (a + b) mod M).
solutions.pseudocode: a = 1; b = 1; repeat length - 1 times: (a, b) = (b, (a + b) mod M); return b
commonMistakes: Applying the modulo only at the end, after values have exceeded the safe integer range.
Off-by-one in the loop bounds, which returns ways(n ± 1).
solutions.interviewExplanation: Splitting on the leftmost column gives ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2), the Fibonacci recurrence. I roll it forward with two variables and reduce modulo 1e9+7 each step. That's O(n) time and O(1) space. Matrix exponentiation would give O(log n) if the length were huge.
